means.en: A group of people held together by kinship and counted as one people. The Ṛigveda names about thirty of them.
The Sanskrit word we still use for king. The English word king is this word with its ending worn away.

plain.en: the hall - and the small council that sat in it

means.en: A small body of selected people whose work was judicial: settling disputes, deciding who was owed what, fixing penalties.
A larger body standing for a much broader share of the population. Its business was policy: what the clan as a whole ought to do.

plain.en: the popular gathering - the whole people

means.en: Not a body of chosen people at all, but the community itself, the clans gathered in one place for war and other public questions.
Five of the clans the Ṛigveda names - Yadu, Turvaśha, Puru, Anu and Druhyu - counted together as one group.

plain.en: priest-scholar - and also a set of Vedic prose texts

means.en: The prose part of each Veda, which explains ritual performances. The same spelling is also used for a varṇa category.
The part of a Veda with the thoughts of sages living in forests. Araṇya means forest.
At first one couple, their children and their blood. As society grew more complicated the word widened to mean a whole household living and moving as a unit.
Several kulas make a grāma. It is the smallest unit of social life, and later also of local government.
The large territorial states that rose in the 6th century BCE, each one ruled over a fixed stretch of land rather than by kinship.
The territory of the state together with the people living on it - the land a king actually rules over.
The rank held above all other crowned kings - a king who claimed to be first among them.

plain.en: a treatise on running a state

means.en: Kauṭilya's treatise on statecraft, one of the earliest and most systematic. It stresses training a king in governance.

plain.en: the field of the wheel-turning king

means.en: The whole world seen as one domain, ruled by a universal king. Kauṭilya equated it with the land between the Himalaya and the sea.
wheel

plain.en: the land of the jujube tree

means.en: An ancient name for the Indian subcontinent, thought of as one island-continent among many.
The earth as a defined territory. Kauṭilya measures it as the land between the Himalaya and the sea.
A Vedic rite in which a horse was let loose and then tracked down and brought back - proof that the king ranged over the whole land.
A Vedic rite a king performed to be invested with kingship over the whole land.
The vernacular languages of north India, as against Sanskrit. Aśhoka cut his edicts in Prakrit so ordinary people could read them.

plain.en: the script of the early inscriptions

means.en: The earliest script of Indian writing, used for Aśhoka's edicts and for the coins and grants of the centuries after him.
The Pāli word for what Sanskrit calls dharma. In a Buddhist text it names the moral ground a ruler is expected to promote.
Two senses: a republican state in early India (gaṇa or saṁgha), and the community of Buddhist monks.
The councillors, ministers and other high officials around the king. Take them away and there is no one to carry out an order.
The treasury, the wealth of the kingdom. Without it there is no revenue and no way to pay anyone.
The forces of defence and of law and order - the power that backs a decision. Also, the stick: punishment itself.
Another king's word for allies. It counts among the limbs of the state because friendship is a resource a kingdom spends.
Fortified towns and cities. A fortified town is one that can be held when the plain around it cannot.
The official who headed the civil administration. A body of them together formed the council of ministers.
An office the Gupta administration added, to handle foreign policy and defence together. It did not replace the civil mantri.
An amātya who served at the local or provincial level. It describes where he worked, not a rank above amātya.

plain.en: giving each unit its own work and its own officers

means.en: The chapter's word for roughly 300 CE to 800 CE. The kingdom was cut into units, and each unit was given its own work - not the king letting go, but the ladder occupied all the way down.
The northern name for the top rung of the administrative ladder. A southern record would call the same rung a manḍala.
The southern name for the same rung as bhukti. Same size of place, two vocabularies - which name you meet tells you which part of the country a record comes from.
The northern name for the rung between province and district. A southern record would call this rung a koṭṭam.
The southern name for a district. In the Chola ladder a manḍalam is cut into valanāḍus, and each valanāḍu into nāḍus.
The northern name for a district. A southern record would call the same rung a nāḍu.
The southern name for a district. Each nāḍu was divided into Urs, the individual villages.
The northern name for the rung one step above a village - about what we would call a tahsīl today.
The southern name for the rung one step above a village. It sits at the same height as a northern vithi.
A division of the Gupta empire, each with its own ministers and its own amātyas. Villages sat below the āḥāras.
The man who led a village. Below the āḥāras sat the villages, and each village had its grāmika.
The officer responsible for judicial and administrative work in a district. Each rung of the ladder has its own job, not a generic one.
Villages granted land to be looked after by Brahmans. Such a grant takes land off a ruler's tax roll and adds it to the grant-holder's.

plain.en: a grant to a Brahman settlement

means.en: Tax-free land given to a settlement of Brahmans. The Chālukyas of Badami made such grants, and Aihole and Badami grew into centres of learning.
In the Tamil ladder the Ur is the smallest unit. Its officer is not sent from the district - the Ur runs itself.
The elected members were split into variyams - one committee per village responsibility, each given one job: the tank, justice, taxes, records.
The Tamil name for village self-government: the village draws on its own strength, like water from its own pot.

plain.en: the village whose election rules were carved in stone

means.en: A tenth-century Tamil inscription at the Vaikunṭha Perumal Temple that records how a village chose its own assembly.
Above the village, a group of villages with a headman set over them.

plain.en: the head of a group of villages

means.en: The officer who stood over a viśha. The name is built straight out of the rung he commanded.
a group of villages
head

plain.en: what holds things in their place

means.en: Not only religion. The dharma of iron is to sink, of wood to float: what a thing is meant to be. The chapter uses it for what holds a society together.
The claim that all bodies are made of the same matter and every consciousness is the same one consciousness appearing.
What a thing actually is - as against ṛita, which is what ought to be. The two words sit side by side in the ritual texts.
The arrangement that keeps nature in balance and human society with it, and upholds moral values.
The chapter's word for a broad category of people. The earliest reference is the Puruṣhasūkta, which names four colours from the body of the first person.

plain.en: the hymn of the first person

means.en: A hymn in Book 10 of the Ṛigveda, and the earliest reference to the four varṇas.
What the early hymn calls the warriors, the second varṇa. They fought wars, protected people and administered justice.
The second varṇa. They fought wars, protected people and administered justice - and were also expected to study, to sponsor sacrifices and to give.
The third varṇa: agriculture, herding animals and trade. They also took part in scriptural study and in sacrifice, and gave to charity.

plain.en: the ones expected to serve the other three

means.en: The fourth varṇa. In practice the śhūdras were also in agriculture, animal husbandry and trade - which is the point the lesson keeps returning to.
Four varṇas branch into a very large number of jātis, and the jātis have no ceiling: migration and a new occupation each open a new one.

plain.en: the family line on the father's side

means.en: A patrilineal lineage or clan, traced back to a common ancestor. A man belonged to his father's gotra, and that gotra decided whom he could marry.

plain.en: marrying only inside your own group

means.en: Nobody has to decree it. It only needs a group to keep choosing the same way, long enough - and then the boundaries hold themselves.
People of different varṇas having children together. The mixture then settles into something of its own.
A span you are in rather than a rank you hold. It divides a single life into four stages; it does not divide one person from another.
The first āśhrama: the pupil under a teacher, before anything else is claimed of them.
The second āśhrama: the adult running a household, which is where the family and its occupations actually sit.
The third āśhrama: the later years withdrawn from the household.
The fourth āśhrama: giving the household up altogether. The idea was already in the Vedic tradition, not invented later.

plain.en: a rite that marks a turning point

means.en: First haircut, marriage, cremation. The sixteen are a sequence - one at a time, in order - not a checklist done all at once.
The number attached to the saṁskāras. The chapter counts sixteen rites that mark the turning points of a life.
The chapter's four goals - dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣha. They are destinations a life moves towards, and a person can hold several at once.
One of the four goals of life: having the means to live. The chapter also uses the word for a settled purpose.
One of the four goals of life. It includes both the wish for pleasure and the wish for what one loves.
One of the four goals of life: getting free of the cycle of birth and death. The chapter singles it out as ethically weighty.
The place a pupil lived and studied beside a teacher - not fed by character or grammar, but by a harvest.
Highly respected, and not what most people assume: a guide who took a student from ignorance towards knowledge.

plain.en: a teacher who knows the text from the inside

means.en: The one who has been through it. Alongside the guru, the other word the chapter uses for a teacher.
The bond between a teacher and a pupil - a line you stand in, which only moves if everyone before you did their part.

plain.en: what is remembered, not written down

means.en: The body of what a society remembers about how it should behave - unlike a grammar, it does not try to be complete or mechanical.
Piṅgala's manual of Sanskrit prosody - how a line of verse is measured.

plain.en: poetry that is also an art of making

means.en: Where the point is not only what is said but how well it is said. A culture that keeps writing poems across centuries of collapsing empires is a culture that keeps something.
One of the three practices a pupil ran every day alongside study and meditation. It trains attention and self-control, not only posture.
A renouncer who travels from place to place rather than settling in one ashram.

plain.en: the one who lives on alms

means.en: A mendicant who depends on what others give him each morning - part of the vocabulary of withdrawal the chapter lists.
A renouncer who works at liberation rather than performing ritual on behalf of others.

plain.en: devotion - a direct path to the god

means.en: A route offering direct connection with the gods without the elaborate rituals prescribed in the Vedas. It grew prominent in the sixth-century Tamil region.
Twelve saint-poets who composed hymns in praise of Viṣhṇu - one stream of Tamil Bhakti.
Sixty-three Śhaiva saint-poets who praised Śhiva - the other stream of Tamil Bhakti.
The label for the stream of devotion addressed to Śhiva, as Vaiṣṇava names the stream addressed to Viṣhṇu.
The chapter's word for a collective of traders, artisans and merchants who shared rules, dues and reputation.
A unit of money in western Indian inscriptions of the first century CE - the kind of coin that carries a punch-mark.
The unit an inscription charges interest in. One pratika a month on the hundred is twelve a year.

plain.en: a larger fraction than a pratika

means.en: The bigger of the two interest units on the Nasik inscriptions. Three-quarters of a paḍika a month on the hundred is nine a year.
A trunk road running north to south down the length of the subcontinent, from the Himalaya to Tamilakam.
A highway running across the north, then down the Ganga.

plain.en: the age of the Tamil academy-poets

means.en: The period in the far south whose poets wrote vast bodies of verse, including whole libraries on akam and puram.
The Sangam poets' name for love and the feelings inside a person looking at the world.
The Sangam poets' name for war, public affairs and political organisation - the other half of the pair.
A Tamil text that gives a four-fold division of society too, and names its groups by what they do.
The Tolkappiyam's name for the first of its four groups, named by the work done rather than by birth.
The Tolkappiyam's second group, named for the work they did rather than for where they were born.
The Tolkappiyam's third group - a functional division, which is what makes it worth comparing with varṇa.

plain.en: Brahmans, often patronised by ruling elites

means.en: The Tolkappiyam's fourth group, and the one where the functional division and the varna division overlap most closely.
A republican state in early India, also called a saṁgha.
A monarchical state, ruled by a king.
The north-western region of the Indus, its five tributaries and the Sarasvatī. The earliest sections of the Ṛigveda were composed here.
The first of the seven constituents of the state in Kauṭilya's list.
Kauṭilya's seven parts of the state: king, ministers, territory, forts, treasury, army and allies.
A small body of elder statesmen whose main role was to advise and support the king.
The Veda that explains how yajñas are performed, with explanations in prose.
Hymns from the Ṛigveda arranged for musical recitation.
Hymns to ward off evil and to treat illness of body and mind.
The part of a Veda with hymns used to call on a deity and make offerings.
The part of a Veda that goes into the Self (Ātman) and the Ultimate Universal Being (Brāhman).
Pottery found in the Ganga region in the first millennium BCE.
A refined ware with a smooth, glossy black surface, from the middle Ganga region.
A term that expressed awareness of the whole land.
A title used by rulers from the 6th century BCE onwards.
The Chera, Chola and Pandya rulers, the three crowned kings of Tamilakam.
An empire of the Deccan that followed the Mauryan Empire and lasted nearly 500 years.
A title of the Chola ruler Rajendra I, to commemorate his conquest of regions along the Ganga.
A northern name for a division of a kingdom, like viṣhaya.
A southern name for a division of a kingdom.
A northern name for a district.
A southern name for a group of villages.
A modern unit: a group of villages under one office.
The contest among the Gurjara-Pratihāras, Pālas and Rāṣhṭrakūṭas.
The root of the word dharma.
A word from the root dhri, to hold or uphold.
A ritual with offerings, most often to the sacred fire.
Giving as a gift.
An early Buddhist collection of verses.
A Sangam poem that describes life and trades.
People moving from one social position or occupation to another.
A person who gives up home and family life to live as an ascetic or wanderer.
Text on stone or metal that dedicates a gift to a deity or sacred place.
Family identity and inheritance passed through the male line.
Working out how much tax is owed.
Mixing cheaper material into a product.
Money placed so that its interest keeps paying for all time.
Someone who looks after money on behalf of others.
A dictionary.
